Successful acquisition of conceptual knowledge

Participants rapidly learned to categorize the training items and successfully generalized this learning to items not presented during training. In both studies, participants categorized training and test items more accurately than expected by chance (50%) in every run, including the first session (one-sample t-tests; Study 1: 𝑡 (61) > 6, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 > 0.763; Study 2: 𝑡 (138) > 9.7, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 > 0.822). Differences from chance were substantial. This suggests that generalizable knowledge about the underlying concepts formed in the first session already.

Importantly, conceptual knowledge continued to improve across tasks and sessions. This was suggested by the fact that categorization accuracy increased across successive training and test runs in both studies (Fig. 2A and B). We assessed these changes using linear mixed-effects models that accounted for repeated measurements within participants. Run number (1-30 for training; 1-9 for testing) was included with linear and quadratic terms, allowing learning trajectories to curve rather than assuming a constant rate of improvement. F-tests assessing the combined linear and quadratic effects of run number indicated significant changes in accuracy in both studies (Study 1, training: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 329.873, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.854; test: 𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 24.487, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.323; Study 2, training: 𝐹 (2, 262.940) = 1314.194, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.909; test: 𝐹 (2, 238.984) = 60.636, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.337), with larger effect-size estimates for training than testing.

Participants also responded faster across successive training and test runs (Figs. S3, S9, and S4). . Model fit errors (C; averaged across exemplar and prototype models) decreased across test runs and sessions, suggesting that participants relied with increasing consistency on relevant features for categorizing items not presented during training; (D) Representational dominance, measured as the difference in model fit errors (prototype minus exemplar), suggested that concept representations were strongly dominated by prototypes rather than exemplar memory (negative dominance value). The prototype dominance increased across sessions for Study 1. Grand means with 95% confidence intervals are plotted for each parameter and study.

Conceptual knowledge progresses more slowly than knowledge about specific training exemplars

We assessed when across days participants reached their individual peak performance levels in training and test runs. We hypothesized that if correct categorization of test items mainly relies on successfully memorized training exemplars, participants should reach peak performance at test at roughly the time when performance peaks in training. However, if additional memory processes are required to promote generalization -such as the integration of exemplar memories into abstract prototype representations -performance on test items may reach its maximum later than performance during training.

To test these alternative hypotheses, we compared the timing of peak performance between training and test runs. For this, we identified the session in which each participant achieved their highest categorization accuracy, separately for training and test runs. Test performance peaked later than training performance in both studies (Fig. 3; main effect of task, Study 1: 𝐹 (1, 118) = 6.398, 𝑝 = .013, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.051; Study 2: 𝐹 (1, 137) = 59.747, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.304). In Study 1, this difference depended on training-set size (interaction between task and training-set size: 𝐹 (1, 118) = 9.889, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.077). Post-hoc comparisons with Holm adjustment showed that test performance peaked significantly later than training performance for the small training set of eight items (𝑡 (59) = 3.892, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 = 1.023). No significant difference was detected for the large training set of 24 items (𝑡 (59) = -0.453, 𝑝 Holm = .652, 𝑑 = -0.112). In Study 2, test performance peaked later than training performance, with no significant evidence that the size of this delay differed between conditions (𝑝 > .325). However, the overall timing of peak performance differed between conditions: averaged across training and testing, peaks occurred earlier when additional category-irrelevant features were present than when stimuli contained only relevant features (main effect of condition: 𝐹 (1, 137) = 4.163, 𝑝 = .043, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.029). These findings suggest that the ability to generalize to test items reaches its peak later than performance on training items. Hence, the memory processes that promote generalization may continue to unfold even when training performance has already plateaued. However, this may only be true when concepts are learned from small training sets. In fact, the difference in peak times was observed only for the small training set in Study 1, and for both distinctiveness conditions in Study 2, where the training sets were always small. In Study 1 (left panel), participants' performance peaked during earlier sessions for training vs. test runs, but only for the small training set (red). In Study 2, training performance peaked in earlier sessions compared to test performance across both conditions. Graphs present the grand means with 95% confidence intervals for the session number (1-5) in which participants' individual categorization accuracy reached the maximum for training and test runs.

Concepts are represented by prototypes rather than exemplars

Participants' categorization behavior was dominated by prototype representations (Fig. 2C and D).

The prototype model fitted participants' responses better than the exemplar model in all nine test runs in both studies (t-tests comparing model fit errors; Study 1: all 𝑡 (61) < -6, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 < -0.775; Study 2: all 𝑡 (138) < -6.696, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 < -0.567). These differences were substantial, with 𝑑 < -0.775 in Study 1 and 𝑑 < -0.567 in Study 2; negative values indicate lower fit errors for the prototype model.

Importantly, the relative influence of prototype representations continued to increase over tasks and sessions in Study 1. We assessed changes across the nine test runs using linear mixedeffects models that accounted for repeated measurements within participants and included linear and quadratic terms for run number, allowing trajectories to curve over time. An F-test assessing the combined effects of these terms indicated a significant change in representational dominance, measured as prototype minus exemplar model fit error (𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 5.480, 𝑝 = .005, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.096). In Study 2, changes in representational dominance depended on the presence of additional category-irrelevant features (see High perceptual distinctiveness impairs memory gen-eralization but promotes prototype dominance below). In the high distinctiveness condition, which used the same stimuli as the small training set condition in Study 1, prototype dominance increased descriptively, but the corresponding F-test did not indicate a statistically significant change across runs (𝐹 (2, 116.294) = 1.535, 𝑝 = .220, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.026). In both studies, model fit errors decreased across successive test runs, indicating that the cognitive models increasingly captured participants' categorization behavior. F-tests assessing changes in model fit error with run number showed significant effects in both studies (Study 1: 𝐹 (2, 109.722) = 30.700, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.359; Study 2: 𝐹 (2, 256.483) = 66.701, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.342). This suggests that participants increasingly relied on category-relevant features for representing the learned concepts and for categorizing test items.

Additional control analyses suggested that the dominance of prototype representations is not an artifact of the stimulus material or the modeling approach. Theoretically, it is conceivable that our modeling approach or the specific stimulus set we used allowed the prototype model to better fit any response pattern in the absence of a true prototype dominance. For example, in our stimulus set, no single stimulus of the test set shared all relevant features with any of the training stimuli.

But multiple test stimuli perfectly matched their prototype. This might provide an advantage for the prototype model. On the other hand, exemplar models generally have greater flexibility and thus tend to provide better fits even to random response patterns [56].

We therefore performed multiple control analyses to assess whether the observed representational dominance reflects a true dominance of prototype representations rather than stimulus-or modeling-inherent biases. These analyses included leave-one-out cross-validations, Monte Carlo simulations, the fitting of mixture models that estimate the relative influence of exemplar and prototype models under the assumption that both can simultaneously guide behavior, and fitting prototype and exemplar models using psychologically plausible multimodal embeddings [57] instead of binary features to represent the stimulus material. In all these control analyses, the overall pattern of results remained unchanged. Specifically, we observed an overall dominance of prototype representations, as well as an increase in prototype dominance across tasks and sessions (for details, see Validation of the computational modeling approach).

Conceptual knowledge evolves offline between daily experimental sessions

Standard theories of human memory posit that memory abstraction and the extraction of conceptual knowledge can occur offline following learning, especially during periods of rest. We therefore examined how conceptual knowledge evolved offline in our studies by assessing the change in categorization behavior between the last training or test run of a session (before the offline period) and the first run of the next session on the next day (after the offline period; see Fig. 4 and supplementary Figs. S1 and S2). Specifically, we assessed how the representational dominance (exemplar vs. prototype) evolved offline. We further examined changes in categorization accuracy and response times for both training and test runs.

Participants' internal representations shifted towards prototypes during offline periods. This was suggested by an analysis of the influence of time (pre-vs. post-offline assessment) on the representational dominance, i.e., the difference between the model fit errors for prototype vs. exemplar models. In Study 1, representational dominance significantly shifted towards prototypes from the pre-to the post-offline period (main effect of time: 𝐹 (1, 413) = 6.179, 𝑝 = .013, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.015). There was some indication that this shift differed between training-set sizes, although the interaction between time and training-set size did not reach statistical significance (𝐹 (1, 413) = 3.458, 𝑝 = .064, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.008). Post-hoc comparisons detected a significant shift towards prototypes for the small training set (𝑡 (413) = 2.980, 𝑝 Holm = .006, 𝑑 = 0.391), whereas no significant shift was detected for the large training set (𝑡 (413) = 0.455, 𝑝 Holm = .649, 𝑑 = 0.056). In Study 2, a similar shift towards prototypes was observed in the high distinctiveness condition, which used the same stimulus set as the small training set condition in Study 1 (effect of time: 𝐹 (1, 469) = 4.624, 𝑝 = .032, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.010, 𝑑 = 0.184). The estimated effect was smaller than in Study 1. No significant shift was detected in the low distinctiveness condition (𝐹 (1, 490) = 0.184, 𝑝 = .668, 𝜂 2 𝑝 < .001). Interestingly, categorization accuracy did not show significant offline changes for either test or training items. This was suggested by analyses in which we assessed categorization accuracy as a function of time (pre-/post-offline), task (training/test) and experimental conditions (training set size and motivational context in Study 1, distinctiveness in Study 2). In both studies, time (pre-/post) did not significantly modulate accuracy, either as a main effect or in interaction with any other predictor (all 𝑝 > .128). Following these nonsignificant results, we conducted an exploratory analysis asking whether observed accuracy increases were more frequent across offline intervals for test than for training items, irrespective of the magnitude of change. For each participant and interval, we classified accuracy changes as increases or no increases, with the latter including unchanged or decreased accuracy. We then used binomial generalized linear mixed-effects models to assess whether the odds of an observed increase differed by task and experimental condition.

In this exploratory analysis, increases were significantly more frequent for test than for training items in the conditions that also showed significant shifts towards prototype representations. This finding concerns the frequency of observed increases rather than their magnitude and does not establish an average offline improvement in accuracy. In Study 1, the difference between training and testing in how frequently accuracy increased across offline intervals depended on training-set size (interaction between time and condition: 𝜒 2 (1) = 5.687, 𝑝 = .017; interaction odds ratio, OR = 0.388). Post-hoc comparisons showed that, for the small training set, the odds of an interval showing increased accuracy were approximately 2.9 times as high for test as for training runs (OR = 2.911, 𝑧 = 3.676, 𝑝 Holm < .001). For the large training set, no significant difference was detected (OR = 1.130, 𝑧 = 0.451, 𝑝 Holm = .652). A similar pattern was observed in Study 2 in the high distinctiveness condition, which used the same stimulus set as the small training set condition in Study 1. In this condition, the odds of an offline interval showing increased accuracy were approximately 2.6 times as high for test as for training runs (𝜒 2 (1) = 22.044, 𝑝 < .001, OR = 2.574). No significant difference between test and training runs was detected in the low distinctiveness condition (𝜒 2 (1) = 0.541, 𝑝 = .462, OR = 1.145). To illustrate these effects, we plotted the mean number of offline periods during which participants showed a gain in accuracy separately for each task, condition, and study (Fig. 4).

Importantly, response latencies showed offline drifts that were consistent with the observation of a shift of internal representations: In both studies, response latencies increased significantly after an offline period for training but not for test items. In Study 1, an F-test indicated a small but significant three-way interaction between time (pre-vs. post-offline), task, and training-set size (𝐹 (1, 885) = 4.680, 𝑝 = .031, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.005). Responses were generally slower during training than testing (effect of task: 𝐹 (1, 885) = 142.035, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.138). Post-hoc comparisons detected a significant offline slowing for training runs in the small training set condition (𝑡 (885) = -4.081, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 = -0.536; negative values reflect the pre-minus-post contrast). No significant offline changes were detected for test runs in this condition or for either task in the large training set condition (|𝑡 (885)| < 0.766, 𝑝 Holm > .999, all |𝑑| < .095). In Study 2, offline changes in response times differed between training and testing in both distinctiveness conditions. In the high distinctiveness condition, an F-test indicated a significant interaction between time and task (𝐹 (1, 1005) = 4.975, 𝑝 = .026, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.005). Post-hoc comparisons detected significant offline slowing for training runs (𝑡 (1005) = -2.383, 𝑝 Holm = 0.035, 𝑑 = -0.204), whereas no significant change was detected for test runs (𝑡 (1005) = 0.7716, 𝑝 Holm = 0.441, 𝑑 = 0.066). A similar pattern was observed in the low distinctiveness condition, with a significant interaction between time and task (𝐹 (1, 1050) = 12.155, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.011). Post-hoc comparisons detected significant offline slowing for training runs (𝑡 (1050) = -4.016, 𝑝 Holm < 0.002, 𝑑 = -0.337), but no significant change for test runs (𝑡 (1050) = 0.915, 𝑝 Holm = 0.361, 𝑑 = 0.077). As in Study 1, negative effect sizes reflect slower responses after the offline interval because contrasts were calculated as preminus post-offline values.

We next examined whether offline changes in representational dominance, categorization accuracy, and response times were associated within participants. We focused on the small training set condition in Study 1 and the high distinctiveness condition in Study 2, where significant offline shifts towards prototype representations had been detected. In both studies, repeated-measures correlations showed that, within participants, offline intervals with larger shifts towards prototype representations were associated with larger increases in test accuracy (Study 1: 𝑟 rm = -.531; Study 2: 𝑟 rm = -.294; both 𝑝 Holm < .001). The negative correlations reflect the coding of representational dominance: more negative changes indicate larger shifts towards prototypes. The corresponding associations with changes in training accuracy were not statistically significant (Study 1: 𝑟 rm = .042, 𝑝 Holm > .999; Study 2: 𝑟 rm = -.179, 𝑝 Holm = .094). In Study 1, larger offline increases in training accuracy were also associated with larger increases in training response times (𝑟 rm = .378, 𝑝 Holm = .003). No other correlations reached statistical significance (all 𝑝 Holm > .183). Thus, offline shifts towards greater prototype dominance were associated with changes in generalization accuracy, despite the absence of a significant average offline increase in accuracy.

In sum, our results suggest that conceptual knowledge continues to evolve offline, between daily experimental sessions. Although prototype models better explained categorization from the first assessment, their relative advantage increased further across offline intervals in the small training set condition in Study 1 and the high distinctiveness condition in Study 2. Within these conditions, larger offline shifts towards prototype dominance were associated with larger increases in test accuracy, despite the absence of a significant average offline improvement in accuracy. An exploratory analysis also found that observed accuracy increases were more frequent for test than for training items in these conditions. Response times increased offline for training items in the small training set condition in Study 1 and in both distinctiveness conditions in Study 2. Together, these findings suggest that offline changes involve the continued refinement of existing prototype-based representations, with larger shifts towards prototype dominance associated with larger increases in generalization accuracy.

Figure 4: Offline evolution of conceptual knowledge

In Study 1 (A) in the small training set condition (red; "small"), we observed offline changes in behavior that indicate an offline transformation of conceptual knowledge. Specifically, we observed that representations shifted towards prototypes (Repr. Dom.: difference in representational dominance, post-minus pre-offline period), observed accuracy increases were more frequent for test than for training runs (Freq. incr.: number of offline intervals during which accuracy showed any increase, irrespective of its magnitude), and response latencies increased for training but not test runs (Resp. time: difference in response latencies, post-minus pre-offline period). Importantly, we replicated these results in Study 2 (B) in the high distinctiveness condition (red; "high"). Grand mean values with 95% confidence intervals are plotted.

Larger training sets do not facilitate acquisition of generalizable conceptual knowledge

In Study 1, we examined how concept knowledge evolves when learning builds on a very limited set of experiences compared to a larger set of distinct experiences. Specifically, we asked how training performance, test performance, representational dominance, and response latencies evolve across runs and sessions when participants practice with only 8 compared to 24 distinct training items (small vs. large training set). Importantly, the number of training opportunities was held constant across conditions by repeating stimuli in the small training set three times per training run.

A larger training set did not yield a detectable advantage in concept generalization (Fig. 5).

Neither mean accuracy on the generalization test nor its evolution across runs and sessions differed significantly between training-set conditions (effect of training-set size: 𝐹 (1, 59) = 1.332, 𝑝 = .253, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.022; interaction with run number: 𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 1.104, 𝑝 = .336, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.021). No significant effects of training-set size were detected for representational dominance (all 𝑝 > .112), model fit errors (all 𝑝 > .237), or response times during testing (all 𝑝 > .083; Fig. S3). During training, however, participants in the large training set condition were less accurate overall (effect of training-set size: 𝐹 (1, 59) = 9.419, 𝑝 = .003, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.138), and their accuracy improved more slowly across runs (interaction between training-set size and run number: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 6.737, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.107). Response times also decreased more slowly during training in the large training set condition (interaction: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 6.434, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.103). In the featureknowledge test administered after the final session, participants in the large training set condition recalled fewer category-specific feature values (𝜒 2 (1) = 7.306, 𝑝 = .007, OR = 1.516 for small relative to large training sets). Recognition accuracy, however, did not differ significantly between training-set conditions (𝐹 (1, 52) = 0.525, 𝑝 = .472, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.010). In sum, increasing the number of distinct training examples while holding the total number of training presentations constant did not yield a detectable advantage in generalization accuracy or significantly promote prototype dominance. This could suggest that successful generalization and internal representations of concepts (exemplar vs. prototype) are mainly determined by the number of training opportunities (which was identical across conditions), not the diversity of experiences (which was larger in the large training set). Interestingly, participants trained with the larger set showed lower training accuracy and slower improvements during training. These differences likely reflect the fewer repetitions of each individual training example in the larger set. It is still possible that the size of training sets influences the trajectory of concept learning. In fact, we observed better recall of category-defining feature values in the small compared to the large training set condition. We also detected a significant offline shift towards greater prototype dominance in the small but not the large training set condition (see Conceptual knowledge evolves offline between daily experimental sessions). Finally, we observed that generalization accuracy progressed more slowly in the small training condition (see Conceptual knowledge progresses more slowly than knowledge about specific training exemplars).

Figure 5: Study 1 -Larger training sets slow training performance gains without a detectable advantage in generalization

Categorization accuracy for training items improved more slowly for the large and more diverse training set compared to the small set (A). However, neither categorization accuracy at test (B) nor model fits (C) nor representational dominance (D) were significantly influenced by training set size. Grand mean values with 95% confidence intervals are plotted.

High perceptual distinctiveness impairs memory generalization but promotes prototype dominance

In Study 2, we assessed how perceptual distinctiveness influences concept learning. We compared learning performance and the relative fit of exemplar and prototype models between stimuli containing both category-relevant and category-irrelevant features (high distinctiveness) and stimuli containing only category-relevant features (low distinctiveness).

Participants in the high distinctiveness condition achieved higher training accuracy and improved more rapidly across training runs (Fig. 6). F-tests indicated significant effects of condition on training accuracy (𝐹 (1, 137) = 8.824, 𝑝 = .004, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.061) and an interaction between condition and run number (𝐹 (2, 262.940) = 6.435, 𝑝 = .002, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.047). During testing, however, participants in this condition showed lower categorization accuracy (𝐹 (1, 137) = 27.405, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.167) and larger model fit errors (𝐹 (1, 137) = 31.881, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.189). The evolution of representational dominance also differed between conditions, with a significant interaction between condition and run number (𝐹 (2, 238.984) = 9.811, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.076). In the high distinctiveness condition, no significant change in prototype dominance was detected across test runs (𝐹 (2, 116.294) = 1.535, 𝑝 = .220, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.026). In the low distinctiveness condition, prototype dominance decreased significantly over time (𝐹 (2, 121.545) = 14.231, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.190). Nevertheless, the prototype model fitted categorization responses better than the exemplar model at every test in both conditions (t-tests: all 𝑝 Holm < .003, all 𝑑 < -0.371). Direct comparisons between conditions at the first test in session 1 and the last test in session 5 further illustrated these different trajectories. At the first test, prototype dominance was significantly greater in the low distinctiveness condition (𝑡 (135.791) = -2.381, 𝑝 Holm = .019, 𝑑 = -0.403). At the last test, the direction of the difference was reversed, with significantly greater prototype dominance in the high distinctiveness condition (𝑡 (128.061) = 3.074, 𝑝 Holm = .005, 𝑑 = .523). No significant effects of condition on response times were detected (all 𝑝 > .071).

Participants in the high distinctiveness condition also showed better knowledge of categorydefining feature values in the feature-knowledge test administered after the final session (Fig. S5).

The odds of correctly recalling a feature value and assigning it to the corresponding family were approximately 25% higher in the high than in the low distinctiveness condition (𝜒 2 (1) = 5.629, 𝑝 = .018, OR = 1.246). Participants in the high distinctiveness condition also identified the family associated with individual feature values more accurately in the recognition task (𝐹 (1, 133) = 4.760, 𝑝 = .031, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.035). These results suggest that high perceptual distinctiveness facilitates memorization of individual training examples, but also promotes prototype learning and the generation of explicit insights into category-defining features, while paradoxically reducing generalization to test items not presented during training.

Figure 6: Study 2 -Influence of perceptual distinctiveness on concept learning

High perceptual distinctiveness (highlighted in red) facilitated learning of training items as indicated by increased accuracy during training runs (A). However, high distinctiveness impaired the transfer to test items (B; lower accuracy) and thus interfered with concept learning. Relatedly, high distinctiveness was associated with worse model fits (C). Prototype dominance decreased over time in the low distinctiveness condition, whereas no significant change was detected in the high distinctiveness condition (D). Prototype models fitted responses better than exemplar models at every assessment in both conditions (negative values in D). Grand mean values with 95% confidence intervals are plotted.

Discussion

We examined how abstract, generalizable knowledge for naturalistic concepts is acquired and evolves over multiple days. For this, we had participants learn to categorize high-dimensional, multimodal cartoon monsters into two families (the concepts) in daily sessions over five consecutive days. We assessed participants' abilities to generalize their knowledge to items not presented during training and fitted cognitive models of category learning to categorization behavior. Participants rapidly generalized in the first session already, and their knowledge continued to improve with further training over the next days. Cognitive modeling suggested that concepts were represented by abstract prototypes rather than memories for unique training exemplars, and that the dominance of prototype representations increased with further training. Importantly, conceptual knowledge continued to evolve offline between test sessions, outside of actual training and test tasks. Specifically, the dominance of prototype representations increased offline. Moreover, observed accuracy increases across offline intervals were more frequent for test than for training items, whereas response latencies slowed offline selectively for training but not test runs.

Our concept learning task promoted the use of prototype rather than exemplar representations for categorizing new items. Importantly, this prototype dominance tended to increase across learning.

Even when concepts were learned with only a few instead of many training exemplars (8 vs.

24), prototype dominance persisted. This is relevant because learning with the smaller training set facilitated the memorization of training exemplars, which in theory should have promoted the use of these exemplars rather than prototypes for categorizing new items at test. Our results thus are in stark contrast to a large body of evidence which suggests that concepts tend to be represented by means of specific memorized exemplars [8, 12, [58] [59] [60], that the influence of exemplar representations increases with training [22, 23], and that small training sets promote exemplar dominance [44, 45]. However, previous work almost unanimously used low-dimensional, unimodal stimuli that contained only category-relevant features, and studied concept learning in single-session experiments only.

We argue that the observed prototype dominance in our studies was due to our use of perceptually unique, multi-modal, high-dimensional stimuli that contained both relevant and irrelevant perceptual features. Removing the irrelevant features in the low distinctiveness condition in Study 2 indeed changed the dominance of prototype representations. When irrelevant features were present, prototype dominance was strong (both studies) and increased across learning (Study 1). When these features were removed (Study 2), prototype dominance was even stronger in the beginning but decreased across learning, as participants formed robust memories for the training exemplars. This latter finding closely matches earlier reports which suggested that exemplar dominance increases with training [22, 23].

Importantly, the presence of category-irrelevant features facilitated learning of training exemplars but impaired generalization to items not presented during training -despite promoting the use of prototype representations at test. This finding may seem paradoxical: How can excellent memory for training exemplars still allow for the formation of prototype representations and encourage the use of these prototypes for categorizing new items? We argue that the high distinctiveness provided by the presence of category-irrelevant features not only facilitated learning of training exemplars but also increased the discriminability between training and test items. Note that each cartoon monster had a unique physical appearance as well as a unique pronounceable name. No two monsters looked alike -even when sharing all category-relevant features. Due to the high distinctiveness between training and test items, participants did not try to directly compare test items to individual training exemplars. Instead, they identified and used abstract rules or prototypes for categorizing new items at test. But they may sometimes have included irrelevant features in their prototype definitions, leading to lower performance at test. This argumentation is supported by studies which suggested that the presence of category-irrelevant features generally impairs categorization [52] [53] [54] but promotes formation of prototypes [13]. Our argumentation further finds support in the observation that exemplar and prototype representations may coexist in the brain [21], and may be used strategically in different contexts.

Conceptual knowledge continued to evolve offline between sessions. Specifically, concept representations shifted further towards prototypes from the last task of a session to the first task of the next session on the following day. Moreover, categorization accuracy showed a higher ratio of offline gains for test compared to training accuracy, and response latencies showed offline slowing for training but not test runs. These findings suggest that offline periods promoted the refinement of abstract and integrated concept representations that were less dependent on the memory for specific training exemplars. Importantly, these significant offline shifts towards prototypes were only observed for the small but not the large training set condition (Study 1), where concept learning was based on only a few distinct training examples (8 instead of 24). In the small training set, the covariance between the perceptual features that are relevant for categorization was less diverse. This may hinder the extraction of abstract, generalizable rules for categorizing new items during training due to overfitting and may call for post-learning memory processes that enable generalization and insight. Additionally, significant offline shifts towards prototypes were observed only for the highly distinct stimuli that contained category-irrelevant perceptual features, not for the low distinctiveness stimuli that only contained category-relevant features (Study 2). High dimensionality may have impeded identification of relevant features and may have promoted overfitting, which again called for post-learning processing to enable generalization.

We argue that offline transformation of conceptual knowledge was enabled by mechanisms that promote memory consolidation during periods of rest and sleep following learning [25] [26] [27] [28]. During rest and sleep, the brain is believed to replay previously acquired memories [29, 30], promoting their integration and the extraction of abstract, generalized representations. This consolidation account is consistent with the observation that offline transformations occurred only in the small, but not the large, training-set condition, that is, when fewer training examples were repeated more often (18 rather than 6 times per session). A recent study showed that repetition during encoding increases the likelihood of subsequent offline replay [61], which in turn may promote generalization and abstraction [62]. Thus, repeated exposure to the same training examples may have increased their probability of offline reactivation and thereby facilitated the transformation of category knowledge. However, because we neither monitored sleep nor tracked spontaneous offline reactivation of memories, we cannot determine whether such consolidation processes were responsible for the observed transformations. Other mechanisms could have contributed as well. For example, selective forgetting of detailed information about the training examples might account for the observed offline changes [63]. Individual training exemplars and irrelevant details are generally more prone to forgetting than abstract prototypes [64, 65]. Assuming that exemplar and prototype representations coexist in the brain [20, 21], selective forgetting of exemplar-specific information may therefore have increased the relative influence of prototype representations on subsequent categorization behavior. Alternatively, participants may have deliberately searched for rules and regularities defining category membership between sessions, potentially leading to insights that boosted performance on the following day. Such explicit search and optimization may have been encouraged by the deferred feedback on average categorization performance provided after each test run [66]. The present data therefore cannot distinguish whether offline transformations arose from spontaneous memory-consolidation processes, differential forgetting, active post-session reflection, or a combination of these mechanisms.

Admittedly, our findings are not without limitations. Although we used naturalistic highdimensional stimuli and a multi-day study design to track the long-term emergence of conceptual knowledge in a more realistic setting than previous studies, our findings may still not fully translate to concept learning in everyday life. For example, we repeatedly used the same training and test stimuli across sessions. But in everyday life, conceptual knowledge often evolves from unique experiences, and it needs to generalize to many unseen events. The generalizability of our findings is further limited by the fact that we clearly labeled training and test tasks. But in everyday life, the distinction between familiar and novel experiences may not always be clear. The transferability of our findings is also limited by the specific concept structure used in our work: participants learned simple, linearly separable categories that contained no exceptions to the rules. But natural concepts often have complicated hierarchical, non-linearly separable structures that include unique exceptions and rare cases. Finally, our primary cognitive-model analyses included only the predefined category-relevant features. This does not directly impair the validity of our findings because irrelevant features were fully counterbalanced across the concepts. However, it limits the generalizability to everyday learning, where experiences are always high-dimensional, and irrelevant features are not counterbalanced across learning examples.

Conclusion

Our work advances our understanding of how humans integrate high-dimensional, multimodal experiences into abstract generalized representations that allow us to make sense of new events and situations. We show that even when only a limited set of training examples is available, repeated training can provide abstract knowledge that generalizes to new situations. The emergence of this knowledge benefits from extensive training even when training performance is already at ceiling. Moreover, this knowledge may continue to evolve offline, possibly during periods of rest and sleep. These findings are consistent with proposed benefits of spaced vs. massed learning: repeated re-learning, testing and feedback across multiple sessions that are distributed over time can enhance long-term retention of the learning material [67] and support memory generalization and abstraction [68], yielding new conceptual knowledge.

Materials and Methods

Participants

Inclusion criteria

In order to participate in our studies, volunteers had to be native or near-native German (both studies) or French (Study 2) speakers and had to have normal or corrected-to-normal hearing levels and vision. Moreover, individuals had to have regular sleep schedules during the time of study participation (no shift work). Only individuals who reported no sleep disorders, no diagnosed memory deficits, and no current episodes of schizophrenia or depression were invited to participate.

Data exclusion

Data were excluded from analysis if participants failed to comply with the study protocol. Main reasons for exclusion were missed or incomplete sessions, taking two sessions in one day, or delaying sessions by one or more days. Data were further excluded if a participant's categorization accuracy never significantly exceeded chance level (50%), based on a cutoff derived from the binomial distribution (one-tailed, 𝛼 = .025), for any of the training or test runs. Finally, data were excluded if a participant's categorization accuracy across all training or test runs was < 50%.

Sample of Study 1

A total of 𝑁 = 83 volunteers signed up for participation in Study 1, of whom 21 had to be excluded from analysis. The final sample consisted of 𝑁 = 62 participants, of whom 42 identified as female, and 20 as male. The mean age was 𝑚 = 33.887 (SD = 10.693, range = [19, 61]).

Sample of Study 2

A total of 𝑁 = 209 volunteers signed up for Study 2, of whom 70 had to be excluded from analysis. The final sample consisted of 𝑁 = 139 participants, of whom 124 identified as female, 13 as male, and 2 as non-binary or undisclosed. The mean age was 𝑚 = 38.065 (SD = 7.692, range = [20, 58]).

Experimental design

In Study 1, the experimental manipulations training set size (small vs. large) and motivational context (gamified vs. neutral) were implemented as a 2×2 between-subjects design. In Study 2, the experimental condition distinctiveness (high: stimuli include relevant and irrelevant features vs. low: relevant features only) was implemented as a between-subjects factor. In both studies, four different stimulus sets with distinct prototypes and stimuli were used in different subsets of participants, counterbalanced across conditions. Stimulus set was treated as a nuisance variable and was not included as a factor in our analyses.

Procedure

General procedure Volunteers signed up for participation via email or through our participant management system. They then received an email with a link to the consent form and to demographic and pre-screening questionnaires. Volunteers who met the inclusion criteria were randomly assigned to one of the experimental conditions and were then asked by email to indicate their preferred starting date for participating in the five daily sessions.

At 5:00 a.m. on each scheduled testing day, participants received an email with the link to the experimental session of the current day. Participants were allowed to complete sessions at their preferred time of day, but were instructed to take each session at about the same time of day, in the same quiet environment, and on the same device (computer or tablet; no smartphones).

Each session started with a brief sleep questionnaire and then proceeded to the actual experiment.

Before continuing with the experiment, a brief audio test was administered to ensure that participants could hear the sound on their computer or tablet. Then, the cover story and instructions for the experiment were presented. Each experiment started with a generalization test, during which we assessed how well participants could transfer their knowledge from the previous sessions to a set of 64 test items that were never shown during training. This test was omitted in the first session.

Next, participants took six feedback-based training runs of 24 trials each. After the second and fourth training runs, brief interim tests with 8 items that were never shown during training or generalization tests were administered. These interim tests aimed at motivating participants to form abstract concept representations. After training run 6, a second generalization test was administered.

After each training and test run, participants were informed about their average accuracy during the previous run. Participants were allowed to take a short break before continuing with the next task.

The context of each task (training/test) was announced before the start. The experiment ended with a brief questionnaire that assessed the intrinsic motivation to participate in the experiment. On the last day, an additional feature knowledge test was administered to assess participants' knowledge of the perceptual features characterizing each monster family. Finally, the participants were debriefed and compensated.

Pre-screening questionnaire Upon signing up for participation, volunteers completed a prescreening questionnaire in which they were asked about their age, level of education, current occupation, and language skills. In this questionnaire, participants were also asked to disclose the current presence of neurological or psychiatric disorders (namely epilepsy, depression, schizophrenia), attention or memory deficits, hearing or vision impairments, sleep disorders, or irregular sleep schedules, e.g., due to shift work. A French translation was provided to French-speaking participants in Study 2.

Sleep questionnaire

At the beginning of each session, participants' subjective sleepiness and the quality of their last night's sleep were assessed using the German version [69] of the Karolinska sleepiness scale [70], the German version [69] of the Epworth sleepiness scale [71], and a single-item sleep quality scale [72]. For French-speaking participants in Study 2, all questionnaire items were translated into French.

Motivation questionnaire

At the end of each session, participants' motivation to partake in the experiment was assessed using the short German version of the intrinsic motivation inventory [73].

For French-speaking participants in Study 2, the questionnaire was translated into French. This scale consists of four subscales that are measured with three items each. The interest/enjoyment subscale assesses how fun and engaging the task is. It is the most direct self-report measure of intrinsic motivation. The competence scale assesses how effective, skilled, or capable a person feels when performing the task. The choice scale relates to autonomy and indicates the sense of freedom to perform the task. The pressure/tension scale indicates the feeling of stress or coercion while performing the task. It is assumed to be a negative predictor of intrinsic motivation.

Task instructions and cover story

Participants were told that in this experiment they must learn to categorize monsters called "Fernis" into two families, the "Brigus" and the "Sidors" that have distinctive sets of visual and auditory features. Participants were instructed to try to identify the relevant features and feature combinations that define each monster family during training runs in order to maximize their categorization accuracy during both training and test runs. The cover story of the experiment was that a bunch of monster babies had just hatched from their eggs in a forest where Fernis go to breed. These hatchlings now need to find their way home to their families. The participants' task was to learn to identify Brigus and Sidors during training runs so that they can then tell the hatchlings in test runs which family they belong to and where they find their home.

Training runs Each trial during training started with a blank screen that was presented for a jittered duration of 500 to 1000 ms. Then, a monster was displayed on the screen, and its name was played in its own voice over loudspeakers. Participants had to indicate the family of the monster on display by clicking on the button of the corresponding family (Fig. 1). The monster was displayed until a participant responded. Upon response, feedback on the accuracy of the response was provided. For correct responses, a rewarding jingle sound was played, and a happy smiley face and a green check mark were displayed in front of a green rectangle. For incorrect responses, an annoying horn sound was played, and a sad smiley face and a red cross mark were shown in front of a red rectangle. The feedback screen was presented for a fixed duration of 2000 ms. Then, the task proceeded to the next trial.

In each of the 6 training runs in a session, 24 items were presented in pseudo-random order.

In the experimental conditions where participants practiced with 8 training examples (small set condition in Study 1, all conditions in Study 2), the 8 items were repeated three times in each training run. Items were repeated in blocks and were presented in a new pseudo-random order for each repetition within a run. In the condition where participants practiced with 24 training examples (large set condition in Study 1), each item was presented only once per run. This yielded a total of 144 training opportunities (24 item presentations × 6 runs) in each session.

Test runs

The sequence of events during test runs was identical to the sequence during training runs (a blank screen followed by a monster stimulus), but no feedback was provided upon response.

In each generalization test run, the same set of 64 test items that were never shown during training was presented in pseudo-random order.

Feature knowledge test

At the very end of the last experimental session, a feature knowledge test was administered which probed participants' knowledge of the category-defining perceptual features. In this test, we first examined whether participants were able to recall the defining feature values of each monster family. For this, we asked participants to list the defining feature values of each monster family in an open-ended question. Then we assessed whether participants could recognize the family that is associated with each feature value of the eight binary features. For this, each feature value was presented on screen one by one (e.g., a picture of monster arms, along with the text label "arms") in pseudo-random order.

For each value, participants had to indicate the corresponding family by clicking the respective button on the screen. No feedback was provided.

This task consisted of 16 trials (two feature values for each of the 8 binary features).

Implementation of game elements in Study 1

Half of the participants in Study 1 were subjected to a gamified version of the concept learning task. In this version, participants were told that they would compete against six other participants who were also performing the task. They were informed that correct responses are rewarded with a point and that they should try to outcompete their opponents by collecting the most points.

The opponents were in fact virtual players whose behavior dynamically adapted to each participant's current performance level in order to keep the task demanding yet rewarding. However, participants were misled into believing that their opponents were actual human participants. This deception was approved by the ethics committee.

At the beginning of each session, the six opponents were introduced with brief vignettes and avatars. Participants were told that they would compete against one of these opponents during each training run, but that they would compete against all six opponents at once during test runs.

Before each training run, the opponent for the next run was introduced. Participants were told that they would see their own score and the opponent's score after each trial. The presentation of training trials was identical to that in the non-gamified, neutral condition. However, the feedback screens that were provided after each response contained information about the accuracy of both the participant's and the opponent's last response and about each player's total score. At the end of a training run, a leaderboard was displayed which showed whether the participant or the opponent won the last run.

Before each test run, participants were informed that they would now have to compete against all six opponents, that no feedback would be presented after a response, but that a leaderboard would be shown at the end. The sequence of events was identical to that in the test runs in the non-gamified, neutral condition.

Whenever a participant won a training or test run, the sound of a cheering crowd was played and the avatar of the player received a trophy. When participants did not win a round, a sad sound was played and the text "You can do better!" was displayed below the leaderboard.

Implementation of online experiments and questionnaires

All experiments were programmed with lab.js [74]. Questionnaires were implemented with LimeSurvey [75]. Experiments and questionnaires were hosted on secure servers at UniDistance Suisse.

Stimulus material

Stimulus properties Stimuli consisted of cartoon monsters that differed on six visual and two auditory binary features that were relevant for categorization. The features and their values are listed in Table 1. The cartoon monsters further differed on a set of features that were not relevant for categorization because the different values within each feature were counterbalanced across families. These irrelevant features included the lightness of the body color (4 levels), the body type (skinny vs.

heavyset, 4 levels), the skin texture (unique set of randomly generated dark skin spots), the type of thorns (4 types: sine waves, triangles, squares, spikes), the length (4 levels) and density (4 levels) of thorns, the hairdo (unique shape), the lightness of the hair color (4 levels of green), the positions of the body parts (the upper and lower extremities, eyes, and oral structure could each vary across 4 levels of vertical position, horizontal position, and orientation), and the name suffix (unique pronounceable three-syllable pseudo-word). Hence, each monster had a unique visual appearance and a unique name. Monsters' names always started with one of two possible prefixes ("NINI" or "DADA") of the relevant binary name feature, and ended with a unique three-syllable suffix (e.g., "kitome"). Monsters' names were presented acoustically and were uttered in one of two possible voices (binary feature voice). For the low distinctiveness condition in Study 2, one fixed value for each of these additional features was used for all monsters. Drawings of cartoon monsters were generated by combining hand-drawn images of body parts with computer-generated images of the main body and hair on a square canvas of 1000 × 1000 pixels. Monsters were scaled to a height of 500 pixels on that canvas.

Stimulus rendering procedure

Audio files for the presentation of the monster names were synthesized using an Italian female voice ("it-IT-Wavenet-B") and a male US voice ("en-US-Neural2-D") from the Google Cloud Text-To-Speech (TTS) API (https://cloud.google.com/text-to-speech).

Category structure

The two monster families were defined by orthogonal prototypes with distinct values for all eight category-defining binary features. From these prototypes, stimuli with varying prototypicality were derived by changing 0, 1, 2, or 3 of the features to the value corresponding to the prototype of the opposite family.

The training set consisted of either four stimuli (small set in Study 1, both conditions in Study 2) or 12 stimuli (large training set in Study 1) per family. Each stimulus differed from its category prototype by two features (prototypicality of 75%). The interim test set consisted of four stimuli per family that all had a prototypicality of 75%. The test set consisted of 32 stimuli per family.

Test stimuli differed from their prototype by either 0, 1, 2, or 3 features, with 8 stimuli per level of deviation. The test set thus included 8 stimuli per family that had prototypical category-defining features but that varied in their individual irrelevant features (except for the low distinctiveness condition in Study 2, where irrelevant features were absent).

The rate at which features deviated from the prototype was identical across features and within families and sets (training, interim test, test). Hence, all features had the same diagnostic value.

Feature combinations were never repeated across training, interim test, and test (except for the 8 prototypical stimuli for each category in the test set).

Feature combinations were manually defined for the Brigu family only and were then derived for the Sidor family by inverting all features to the opposite value. A full list of stimulus definitions for the Brigu family is provided in the supplementary tables S2 , S3, and S4.

Stimulus sets

We generated four different stimulus sets that were each defined by different pairs of orthogonal prototypes. The prototypes for the Brigu family of each set are presented in Table 2.

The corresponding opposite prototypes for the Sidor family were obtained by inverting each binary feature value (e.g., {1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1} for the Sidor prototype for Set 0). Individual stimuli were then generated using the same logic as for set 0, i.e., by inverting specific feature values from the prototype as listed in supplementary tables S2 , S3, and S4.

Feature values correspond to the binary feature coding described in Table 1.

Exemplar and prototype model fitting

We fitted formal models of exemplar-and prototype-based concept representations to participants' behavior in the generalization test. The prototype model posits that humans form one abstract, prototypical representation for storing a concept. New items are classified as members of that category if they exhibit high perceived similarity to the stored prototype. In contrast, the exemplar model assumes that humans categorize by comparing new items to specific examples stored in memory. A new item is classified into a category if the sum of the perceived similarities to all memorized examples of that category is high. In both models, perceived similarity depends not only on physical similarity (e.g., the number of shared features) but also on the attention given to each feature (attentional weights 𝑤) and the discounting of items with low perceptual similarity (sensitivity 𝑐 in an exponential decay function). Formally, the perceived similarity between a test item 𝑥 and the memorized items 𝑦 (eq. 1) or the prototype proto (eq. 2) of a category 𝐴 is defined as follows for the exemplar model [11] and the prototype model [44], respectively (eq. 1 vs. eq. 2): where 𝑥 𝑖 , 𝑦 𝑖 , and proto 𝑖 represent the specific feature values of the 𝑖 th dimension of all 𝑚 binary features of the test item 𝑥, the training item 𝑦, and the prototype proto, 𝑤 𝑖 represents the specific attentional weight assigned to feature 𝑖, 𝑐 represents the sensitivity, and 𝑟 is the distance metric which is fixed at 𝑟 = 1 for binary features.

Prototype feature values were fixed to the categorydefining prototypes, and exemplar representations comprised the distinct training items presented to each participant. The probability 𝑃( 𝐴|𝑥) that a new item 𝑥 belongs to category 𝐴 is calculated by dividing the item's similarity to category 𝐴 by the sum of its similarities with all categories (here: 𝐴 and 𝐵):

To quantify how well a model with specific values for 𝑤 and 𝑐 predicts a participant's behavior, we calculated a negative log-likelihood error measure by taking the negative of the sum of the logarithms of the estimated probabilities that the model assigns each item 𝑥 𝑖 to the same category as the participant: where 𝑛 is the total number of test items, 𝑅 𝑗 is the participant's response to item 𝑥 𝑗 , i.e., the category (𝐴 or 𝐵) to which they assigned the item, and 𝑃(𝑅 𝑗 |𝑥 𝑗 ) is the model's predicted probability that 𝑥 𝑗 belongs to the category assigned by the participant.

To fit a model to a participant's behavior, we optimized the parameters 𝑐 and 𝑤 to obtain a minimal model fit Error, i.e., to find the best possible prediction of behavior based on stimulus features and model assumptions. Feature weights were constrained to be positive and sum to one.

Sensitivity was bounded between 10 -12 and 700. Parameters were optimized using the L-BFGS-B algorithm implemented in R's optim function [76]. The resulting error value was used as an index for how well each model can predict behavior. The model with the better fit (lower error) was assumed to dominate behavior. Representational dominance was thus defined as: where negative values indicate dominance of prototype representations, positive values indicate exemplar dominance, and 0 suggests no clear dominance or equal fits.

Model fitting was conducted in R [76], using custom code inspired by Bowman [77].

Models were fitted to the single-trial data of test runs separately for each participant and each single test run (pre-and post-training test runs for each session; 9 fits per model per participant). In the primary analyses, models were fitted using only the 8 binary features relevant for categorization.

The irrelevant features were ignored. The reasons for this were manifold. First, we were interested in how well participants learned to identify and use relevant features in order to categorize items.

Moreover, the irrelevant features were generally less salient, less verbalizable, and were counterbalanced across families for both training and test items. They were thus truly non-diagnostic of families and are therefore treated as random noise. Importantly, the irrelevant features were introduced to create a more naturalistic setting where each exemplar of a family represents a unique, memorizable identity (e.g., the names). The features were not created with the intention of using them for model fitting. In fact, they were not suitable for use with our model fitting procedure, because they were sometimes not binary but ordinal or categorical, were undefined for the abstract prototypes, and were overall too large in number. Moreover, the raw features used for stimulus generation could interact non-linearly to create unique perceptual properties. Hence, they did not necessarily represent clearly distinct one-dimensional perceptual properties -unlike the diagnostic binary features.

Data preprocessing

Some participants appeared to reverse the family labels in individual generalization tests, resulting in performance significantly below chance. They rapidly corrected their mistake in the first training run that followed. We identified these participants and tasks based on the following rules: accuracy in the task was significantly below chance level (𝑝 < .001) according to a binomial test, and accuracy deviated by more than 2 standard deviations from the average accuracy in all other test runs. For these tests, we reversed the two family labels in participants' responses and recalculated accuracy.

To assess the evolution of categorization accuracy across tasks and sessions, we calculated the ratio of correct responses separately for each task, run, and session for each participant. To analyze response latencies, we calculated the median response time for correct responses within each run and applied a log10 transformation to these medians.

To contrast the time of peak performance between training and test runs, we identified the session number (1-5) in which each participant reached the highest categorization accuracy separately for training and test runs.

To examine whether conceptual knowledge evolved offline, we assessed how categorization accuracy, response latencies, model fits, and representational dominance changed from the last task of a session to the first task of the next session. For these analyses, we only kept the data from the last training runs (run 6) and test tasks of sessions 1 to 4, and from the first training runs and test tasks of sessions 2 to 5. We then labeled the tasks based on their time of administration relative to the offline periods (pre-or post-offline task) and based on the specific offline period (1-4). In an exploratory analysis, we also counted, separately for training and testing, the number of offline intervals during which each participant's accuracy increased. Any positive change was classified as an increase, whereas unchanged or decreased accuracy was classified as no increase. This measure captures the frequency of observed increases irrespective of their magnitude.

To assess participants' knowledge of the category-defining features, we counted the number of correctly recalled feature values for each category from the open-ended questions of the feature knowledge task. We predefined a coding framework to perform a deductive content analysis of participants' open-ended descriptions of the defining features of each category. This allowed us to count the total number of correctly recalled features, which yielded a feature recall score ranging from 0 (no features were recalled) to 16 (all feature values were recalled and correctly attributed to the corresponding category). We additionally calculated feature recognition accuracy as the ratio of single feature values that were correctly attributed to the corresponding category in the ensuing item-by-item test.

Statistical analysis

To assess the temporal evolution of categorization accuracy, model fits, representational dominance, and response latencies across task runs, we fitted linear mixed models with fixed effects for task number (modeled as a second-order polynomial), condition (between-subjects factor), and the interaction between task number and condition, and with random intercepts as well as random slopes for task number (modeled as a linear effect) for participants: where DV denotes the dependent variable.

Task number ranged from 1 to 30 for training runs (5 sessions with 6 runs each), and from 1 to 9 for test runs (first session with one test, sessions 2 to 5 with 2 tests each).

To contrast the time of peak performance between training and test runs, we performed linear mixed model analyses with the session number (1-5) indicating each participant's time of peak performance as the dependent variable, with task (training vs. test), condition, and their interaction as fixed effects, and with random intercepts for participants:

To assess offline changes in categorization accuracy, model fits, representational dominance, and response latencies, we fitted linear mixed models with fixed effects for time (pre-vs. postoffline), offline period (1-4), condition (between-subjects factor), task (training vs. test; only for accuracy and response latencies) and their interactions, and with random intercepts for participants:

In an exploratory analysis, to assess whether the ratio of offline gains differed between training and test runs, we fit binomial generalized linear mixed-effects models with the number of gains and no gains across offline periods as the dependent variables, with fixed effects for task, condition, and their interaction, and with random intercepts for participants:

For Study 1, experimental conditions were motivational context (game/neutral) and training set size (large/small). Note that we did not model interactions between these conditions. Study 2 only had the condition distinctiveness. All statistical analyses were performed in R [76]. We used onesample t-tests to compare categorization and feature-recognition accuracy against chance (50%), and to compare prototype-minus-exemplar model fit differences against zero. Within-participant associations between offline changes were assessed using repeated-measures correlations implemented in the rmcorr package [78]. These correlation analyses were restricted to the small training set condition in Study 1 and the high distinctiveness condition in Study 2, where significant offline shifts towards prototype representations had been detected. Holm correction was applied across the ten pairwise correlations within each study.

Linear mixed model analyses and generalized linear mixed model analyses were conducted with the R package lme4 [79]. Statistical significance of fixed effects in linear mixed models was assessed using Type III F-tests with Satterthwaite-approximated degrees of freedom, as implemented in the lmerTest package [80]. For binomial generalized linear mixed-effects models, fixed effects were assessed using Type III Wald chi-square tests; for the binomial generalized linear models of feature recall, we used Type III likelihood-ratio chi-square tests. Effect sizes were estimated with the effectsize package [81]. Post-hoc contrasts were performed with the emmeans package [82]. P-values for sets of related comparisons were adjusted using the Holm method to control the family-wise error rate [83] pattern, and then (4) normalizing the observed difference in model fits by the distributions of differences drawn from random response patterns. While we approve of the logic behind the use of Monte Carlo simulations, we believe that the proposed implementation has one big disadvantage: the permutation of participants' responses controls for their response biases (i.e., how often they preferred one response over the other), but not for their response accuracy.

But accuracy has a strong systematic influence on model fits and the difference between model fits, whereas response bias does not (Fig. S6). In fact, model fits nonlinearly improve with response accuracy in both true and simulated or permuted data, and the differences in model fits show an increasing dominance of exemplar models with increasing accuracy. Importantly, randomly shuffling participants' responses tends to lead to response patterns with lower accuracy, and hence worse model fits and biased distributions of the differences in model fits.

To overcome this limitation, we implemented an alternative permutation-based approach to correct for model-and stimulus-inherent biases: (1) we simulated multiple random response patterns at all possible levels of response accuracy (1000 per accuracy level, or as many as possible; total number of data sets: 𝑁 = 61131), (2) fitted both models to each random data set, (3) computed the distributions for the differences between model fits at each accuracy level, and (4) normalized each observed difference in model fits by the distribution of differences drawn from random response patterns at the accuracy level of the true data. Normalization consisted of subtracting the mean simulated dominance at the corresponding accuracy level and training-set size, and dividing by its simulated standard deviation. We then used this permutation-normalized representational dominance to validate our original findings.

The distributions of model fits and the differences in model fits calculated for the simulated random response patterns are displayed as a function of response accuracy and response bias in Fig. S6. For both the small and large training data sets, simulations suggested a systematic bias towards the exemplar model (large set: 𝑡 (61130) = 69.268, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 = 0.280; small set: 𝑡 (61130) = 69.667, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 = 0.282).

Analysis of the impact of the motivational context in Study 1

In Study 1, we also aimed to investigate how the motivational context shapes the acquisition of novel concepts. In everyday life, concept learning is often motivated by goals: Humans are motivated to acquire new concepts because this knowledge enables them to understand and act effectively in relevant situations. The motivational context in which learning occurs may therefore influence how rapidly and successfully a concept is acquired, and potentially how it is represented.

Consistent with this possibility, some studies have found that rewarding correct categorizations, rather than providing neutral corrective feedback, facilitates concept learning [84, 85] and promotes the formation of prototype representations [86]. However, other studies have found no evidence for superior learning under reward-based compared with neutral conditions [87, 88]. How motivational context influences the long-term development of conceptual knowledge therefore remains poorly understood. We examined the role of motivation by comparing concept learning in gamified and neutral contexts. Gamification -which involves adding game elements such as points, rewards, and leaderboards to non-game contexts -has been found to increase motivation [89] and improve learning outcomes across a variety of settings [90] [91] [92] [93]. Yet, to the best of our knowledge, whether gamification influences motivation and the acquisition and representation of conceptual knowledge has not been investigated.

Gamified context reduces task interest without a detectable benefit to concept learning

In Study 1, half of participants were subjected to a gamified version of the concept learning task, in which they had to compete against other virtual participants during training and testing. Participants in the control group performed the task without the additional competitive game elements. At the end of each experimental session, we assessed participants' intrinsic motivation to perform the experimental tasks using a short version of the intrinsic motivation inventory [73] that builds on Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory [94]. This scale measures participants' perceived interest in and enjoyment of the task, the perceived competence at performing the task, the freedom of choice to participate in the task, and the perceived pressure or tension when performing the experiment.

Gamification elements failed to improve intrinsic motivation (Fig. S7). Overall, participants' interest in the tasks decreased across sessions (main effect of session: 𝐹 (2, 88.368) = 17.887, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.288), indicating a loss of motivation to continue with the experiment. However, the perceived competence increased (𝐹 (2, 86.945) = 16.795, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.279), while the perceived pressure decreased (𝐹 (2, 82.379) = 24.560, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.374). No significant change in freedom of choice was detected (𝐹 (2, 87.351) = 1.284, 𝑝 = .282, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.029). Interestingly, participants who learned the concepts in a gamified context generally reported lower interest in the task (main effect of context: 𝐹 (1, 58.897) = 5.427, 𝑝 = .023, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.084). This suggests that gamification undermined intrinsic motivation. However, participants in the gamified condition also showed a steeper decline in the perceived pressure across sessions (interaction between context and session: 𝐹 (2, 82.378) = 4.948, 𝑝 = .009, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.107). This could indicate either a more indifferent attitude towards the task, as is also indicated by the lower general interest, or greater familiarity or reduced anxiety. Competence and freedom of choice were not significantly modulated by the motivational context (gamified vs. neutral: all 𝑝 > .174).

Importantly, gamification had no significant impact on concept learning (Fig. S8 and S9). Neither training nor test accuracy, nor model fits or representational dominance were significantly modulated by the context (gamified vs. neutral; all 𝑝 > .068). However, response latencies during testing (𝐹 (1, 59) = 5.939, 𝑝 = .018, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.091) but not training (all 𝑝 > .292) were significantly shorter in the gamified condition. This more rapid responding might reflect facilitated accessibility or processing efficiency of the acquired conceptual knowledge. Alternatively, it could also mirror the overall lower interest in the task. To assess this possibility, we added within and between participant variation in intrinsic interest as predictors of response latencies across generalization tests, adjusting for session and experimental conditions. The effect of gamification remained significant (𝐹 (1, 56.706) = 4.652, 𝑝 = .035, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.076) when controlling for interest. Moreover, participants responded more slowly in sessions when their reported interest was higher than their own average (𝐹 (1, 392.310) = 16.645, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.041). No significant association was detected between participants' average interest and response latencies (𝐹 (1, 58.761) = 0.294, 𝑝 = .590, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.005). Thus, the association between gamification and faster test responses persisted after adjustment for reported interest. Faster responding may reflect facilitated access to conceptual knowledge or greater processing efficiency, although the present analyses do not establish the underlying mechanism.

In sum, using a gamified environment failed to generally improve motivation and learning success. These findings suggest that the particular combination of game elements used here did not improve task interest or categorization accuracy. Evidence for the benefits of game elements

Negative prototype-minus-exemplar fit errors favor prototypes. Pre-minus-post dominance contrasts are positive for shifts towards prototypes; response-time contrasts are negative for slowing. Correlations use post-minus-pre changes.

Odds ratios (ORs) compare the odds of an outcome between two groups. In comparisons written as "testing / training," training is the reference: OR > 1 indicates higher odds during testing. For feature recall, the outcome is correctly recalling a feature value and assigning it to its family. For accuracy increases, the outcome is any increase across an offline interval, regardless of its size. The interaction OR compares the testing-versus-training odds ratio between training-set sizes: it is the large-set OR divided by the small-set OR.

Simulation comparisons use generated response patterns, not participants. Overall-preference tests assess mixedmodel intercepts across test runs; negative values favor prototypes. Prediction-accuracy contrasts use exemplar minus prototype accuracy, so negative values also favor prototypes. Offline validation tests refer to the small training set in Study 1 and high distinctiveness in Study 2. Validation p-values are unadjusted. The nine prototype-favoring approaches are the primary and normalized binary fit errors, full-data and cross-validated binary prediction accuracy, both cross-validated embedding measures, and the three mixture measures. Significant additional offline comparisons comprise normalized binary fit error and both shared-weight mixture measures in Study 1, and the distinct-weight mixture measure in Study 2.

Validation of the computational modeling approach

We performed several control analyses to assess whether the reported dominance of prototype representations could be explained by stimulus-or modeling-inherent biases. To this end, we first calculated several alternative or normalized measures of representational dominance, which are outlined below.

Permutation-based normalization of representational dominance

A frequently used method to correct for potential model-and stimulus-inherent biases when comparing the fits of exemplar and prototype models is permutation testing [56]. This method is usually implemented by (1) randomly shuffling the responses of a participant multiple times, (2) fitting both models to the shuffled response patterns, (3) computing the difference in model fits for each random response 0 20 40 60 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 Accuracy Model fit Model | Set prototype | prototype exemplar | small exemplar | large A) Model fit by accuracy 0 20 40 60 0.5 0.6 0.7 0.8 0.9 1.0 Bias Model fit Model | Set prototype | prototype exemplar | small exemplar | large B) Model fit by bias -0.5 0.0 0.5 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 Accuracy Pr. << Dominance >> Ex.
