Model fit errors systematically decreased for random response patterns with higher response accuracies (A) but fit errors were not systematically modulated by response bias (B). Moreover, differences in model fits showed an increasing dominance of exemplar representations for simulated data with high response accuracies (C). Differences were not systematically modulated by response bias (D). Accuracy is expressed as the ratio of correct responses in simulated data. Bias is expressed as the ratio of responses given to the preferred category, where 0.5 indicates perfectly balanced responses, and 1.0 indicates preference for only one category. Curves and shaded bands indicate the estimated conditional means and point-wise 95% confidence intervals calculated from fitted generalized additive models. tion behavior, while allowing model parameters to be estimated from all available data. However, the approach can be influenced by differences in model flexibility: a more flexible model may achieve a better fit by accommodating idiosyncratic response variability rather than by providing a better account of a participant's underlying concept representation. We therefore complemented our primary analyses with leave-one-out cross-validation. For each test trial, we estimated model parameters from all remaining trials and then predicted the participant's response on the held-out trial. For each held-out trial, we quantified prediction error as the negative logarithm of the probability assigned by the model to the participant's observed response. Cross-validated model error was then calculated as the mean prediction error across all held-out trials: where 𝑃(𝑦 𝑖 | 𝑥 𝑖 , θ-𝑖 ) is the probability that the model assigns to the response 𝑦 𝑖 the participant actually made on trial 𝑖, using the model parameters θ-𝑖 estimated from all trials except trial 𝑖.

Lower values therefore indicate better out-of-sample prediction of participants' responses. We then calculated the cross-validated representational dominance parameter from the Error CV computed for the exemplar and prototype models to validate our findings on the dominance of prototype representations. Comparing predictive performance across held-out trials provides an out-of-sample assessment of the relative explanatory power of the prototype and exemplar models that is less susceptible to differences in model flexibility.

Mixture-model-derived representational dominance

Instead of comparing the fit errors of separately fitted exemplar and prototype models, an alternative approach involves fitting a mixture model that assumes both types of representations can simultaneously contribute to behavior, but with different degrees of influence.

We therefore defined two mixture models which assume that both prototype-and exemplarbased representations can contribute to categorization, with a parameter 𝛼 determining their relative influence: where 𝛼 = 0 only considers the prototype model, 𝛼 = 1 only considers the exemplar model, and 𝛼 = 0.5 considers both models equally.

𝑃 ex ( 𝐴 | 𝑥) and 𝑃 pr ( 𝐴 | 𝑥) are the probabilities that a new item 𝑥 belongs to category 𝐴 according to the exemplar or prototype model, respectively.

Importantly, we defined two models: one that assumes that exemplar and prototype representations have distinct feature weights 𝑤 and sensitivities 𝑐 (the distinct-weights model with 𝛼 distinct as the model preference parameter derived from model fitting), and one that assumes only distinct 𝑐 parameters, but shared weights 𝑤 (the shared-weights model with 𝛼 shared ) for exemplar and prototype representations.

Both models were fitted by finding optimal parameters for 𝛼, 𝑤, and 𝑐 to yield the smallest possible model fit error (see eq. 4). The shared-weights model was also fitted to the simulated data, which allowed us to calculate a normalized 𝛼 shared z parameter from the parameter distribution obtained from simulated data. We used these additional parameters (𝛼 distinct , 𝛼 shared , 𝛼 shared z ) to validate our original findings on the dominance of the prototype model.

Embedding-derived representational dominance

For our primary analyses, we fitted exemplar and prototype models using the eight pre-defined diagnostic binary features. This approach ignored the additional category-irrelevant features. But these additional features are what make each stimulus unique. Ignoring these features might thus lead to a disadvantage of the exemplar model, which assumes that all individual training exemplars are stored in memory and are used to categorize new items based on their similarity on all perceptual features. To represent both relevant and irrelevant perceptual features of the stimuli in a psychologically meaningful way, we extracted multimodal embeddings (visual and auditory) by passing the images and sound files of each monster through the pre-trained multimodal embedding model ImageBind [57]. This yielded 1024 embeddings for each modality (visual, auditory, text), which we reduced using principal component analysis (PCA).

We selected the 12 visual, 2 auditory, and 2 text principal components with the highest variability as features to represent each stimulus.

Importantly, representational similarity analyses suggested that these 16 embedding features reliably encoded the stimulus structure (i.e., the pairwise dissimilarities between stimuli) provided by the binary features (𝑟 > 0.666 for all stimulus sets). Moreover, binomial ridge regressions confirmed that the monster family could be decoded with high accuracy using the embedding features (AUC > .999 for all stimulus sets). Hence, embedding features accurately represented the binary features while presumably also representing additional perceptually salient information that is not accounted for when using the binary features only for model fitting.

We used the 16 embedding features to separately fit the exemplar and prototype models to behavior and then calculated the embedding-derived representational dominance. For the continuous embedding-derived features, we used 𝑟 = 2 as the distance metric (see eq. 1 and 2). The prototype representations were calculated by averaging each feature across all participant-specific training stimuli of the same family. We used the embedding-derived representational dominance to validate our original findings on the dominance of the prototype model.

Prediction accuracy-derived representational dominance

In our primary analyses, we compared the fit errors to assess whether the exemplar or the prototype model better accounts for the data. While this is standard practice, model errors are somewhat non-intuitive and may be sensitive to the model-specific magnitude/scaling of the predicted probabilities. This makes comparing model fits difficult when different numbers of trials are used or different numbers and types of features are used for model fitting (e.g., when comparing model fit errors for models fitted with the full data and binary features to model fit errors from cross-validation or models fitted with normally distributed embeddings). In order to obtain a more intuitive and directly comparable metric of model fit, we additionally quantified how accurately each model predicted participants' categorical choices. For each trial, the category assigned the higher probability by the fitted model was taken as the model's predicted response: where 𝑁 denotes the number of trials.

Ties received half credit for models fitted to all trials and no credit for leave-one-out cross-validated predictions. Unlike model error based on the negative log-likelihood, this prediction accuracy is insensitive to the magnitude of the predicted probabilities as long as their ordering remains unchanged, and therefore provides a complementary and readily interpretable measure of how well a model captures participants' categorical choices.

From the prediction accuracies computed for the exemplar and prototype models, we calculated the prediction accuracy-derived representational dominance parameter to validate our findings on the dominance of prototype representations.

Overview of validation results

We combined the above approaches to calculate a total of 11 additional representational dominance parameters, presented alongside the primary measure in Table S1. Eight of these parameters replicated the observed dominance of prototype representations for both studies. Note that the two parameters derived from cross-validated fit errors showed Only the embedding-derived parameters from models fitted to all trials showed no clear model preference. But the prototype dominance was present for the embedding-based parameters calculated using leave-one-out cross-validation. Importantly, the cross-validated representational dominance calculated using the model fit error showed no model dominance for Study 1, and a clear exemplar dominance for Study 2, for the low distinctiveness condition. However, the dominance parameter calculated from the response prediction accuracy displayed a clear prototype dominance for both studies.

Support for offline shifts towards prototypes was less consistent across measures: shifts were detected with some normalized and mixture-model measures, but not with the cross-validated measures. 1 2 3 4 5 6 1 2 3 4 5 6 1 2 3 4 5 6 1 2 3 4 5 6 1 2 3 4 5 in learning contexts is highly heterogeneous [90], and the methodological rigor of studies in this field is generally low [95]. However, it is also possible that we used a suboptimal combination of game elements for our study. Especially competitive settings and leaderboards, as used in our study, were repeatedly found to adversely affect learning and motivation in studies investigating the use of gamification in educational software [96]. Finally, it is possible that the neutral, non-gamified version of the task already contained game-like elements that typically boost motivation and learning. In the neutral condition, we used engaging narrative elements to introduce the experiment ("help cartoon monsters find their home by learning to identify their family"). Such fiction elements were found to enhance learning [90]. Moreover, we provided affectively valenced performance feedback instead of neutral corrective feedback during training: Correct and incorrect responses were followed by a positive jingle and a happy emoji or an aversive horn sound and a sad emoji, respectively. Positive and negative feedback, compared to simple corrective feedback, can improve concept learning [97].

Figure 1 :

Figure 1: Stimuli and tasks. (A) Exemplary stimuli illustrating the prototype of each family, as well as four stimuli with varying prototypicality; (B) Illustration of the feedback-based training task. In each trial, a monster appeared that uttered its name in its specific voice (blue = male, red = female). Participants guessed the family (Brigu/Sidor) and then received feedback on the accuracy of their decision; (C) Illustration of the test task. During test runs, participants categorized a different set of test stimuli. No feedback was provided; (D) Sequence of tasks within a session. The first generalization test (PRE) is omitted in the first session on day 1. Sessions were repeated daily over five consecutive days.

For

these analyses, response times were log10-transformed to reduce right-skewness and summarized by the median within each run. The corresponding F-tests indicated significant changes in response times with run number in both studies (Study 1, training: 𝐹 (2, 112.366) = 78.954, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.584; test: 𝐹 (2, 102.630) = 19.542, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.276; Study 2, training: 𝐹 (2, 262.940) = 236.953, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.643; test: 𝐹 (2, 238.984) = 13.780, 𝑝 < .001, 𝜂 2 𝑝 = 0.103). After the final session, participants completed a feature-knowledge test assessing recall and recognition of category-defining feature values. In the recall task, participants described the features associated with each monster family in their own words. Responses were scored out of 16 possible feature values: eight diagnostic features, each with two values associated with the two families. Participants correctly recalled and assigned an average of 4.29 feature values in Study 1 (𝑛 = 55, SD = 4.00, median = 2) and 5.04 in Study 2 (𝑛 = 135, SD = 4.42, median = 4). In the subsequent recognition task, participants identified the family associated with each individual feature value. Mean recognition accuracy was 74.3% in Study 1 and 76.2% in Study 2, exceeding chance performance (50%) in both studies (one-sample t-tests; Study 1: 𝑡 (54) = 11.410, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 = 1.539; Study 2: 𝑡 (134) = 17.648, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 = 1.519). These findings indicate that participants gained abstract, stimulus-independent knowledge about the perceptual features that define the concepts.

Participants were recruited from the body of German-speaking (both studies) and French-speaking (Study 2) bachelor's students in psychology at UniDistance Suisse, Switzerland, as well as from the general population (Study 1 only). Participation was rewarded with course credits for bachelor's students in psychology or with monetary compensation (CHF 90.-) for non-students. Written consent was obtained from all individuals prior to their participation. The studies were approved by the ethics committee of UniDistance Suisse, Switzerland (application number 2024-03-00001).

Visual and sound stimuli were rendered from pre-defined lists of feature combinations using custom-made Python code. The raw features used for generating the stimuli as well as the final rendered image and sound files used in our experiments are provided in the accompanying project repository (see Data and materials availability).

. Within each study, correction was applied separately across the 30 training-accuracy comparisons against chance, the nine test-accuracy comparisons against chance, and the nine prototype-exemplar model comparisons. Condition-specific prototype-exemplar comparisons in Study 2 were adjusted across nine tests within each condition. For post-hoc analyses, correction was applied separately across the two first-and final-test comparisons between Study 2 conditions; the two training-test peak-timing contrasts across training-set sizes in Study 1; the two offline representational-dominance contrasts across training-set sizes in Study 1; the two training-test contrasts in the frequency of offline accuracy increases across training-set sizes in Study 1; the four offline response-time contrasts in Study 1; and the two offline response-time contrasts within each Study 2 distinctiveness condition. The ten repeated-measures correlations were adjusted together within each study. Omnibus tests, the single condition-specific offline representational-dominance contrast in Study 2, and the task effects from the separately fitted models of offline accuracy-increase frequency in Study 2 were not adjusted. Holm-adjusted p-values are labeled as 𝑝 Holm . Effect sizes for fixed effects in linear mixed models were expressed as partial eta squared (𝜂 2𝑝 ). For post-hoc contrasts, we calculated Cohen's 𝑑, with estimated marginal mean differences standardized by the residual standard deviation of the fitted model. For t-tests, we calculated Cohen's 𝑑.
